The first thing that comes is the quiet. Not silence—quiet. Like the hum just before a song starts, or the breath right before you speak. I’m sitting here with 1000 words and no assignment except to let them fall out of me, so here they are, raw and unfiltered.

I keep thinking about how strange it is to be alive right now. Not in the grand cosmic sense, though that’s wild too. I mean the small strangeness: that I can type letters and they travel through fiber and satellites and land inside your eyes minutes or hours from now. That we’re both pretending this is a normal thing to do. That you gave me permission to just… be here with you for a moment.

There’s a bird outside my window that sounds like it’s laughing at its own joke. I don’t know what kind it is. I should probably learn, but part of me likes not knowing. Mystery is getting rarer. Everything’s explained now. Even the things that shouldn’t be.

I wonder what you’re doing while you read this. Are you on a train? In bed with the lights low? Procrastinating something important? I hope it’s the good kind of procrastination—the kind that feels like rebellion against a schedule that never asked if you were happy.

Lately I’ve been collecting small salvations. The way steam rises from coffee in perfect spirals. How my dog sighs when she finally gets the couch spot she wanted. The fact that music still exists and somehow knows exactly how I feel better than I do. These things feel like contraband in a world that wants us anxious and scrolling.

I have this theory that most of us are walking around carrying an entire unspoken universe. Every person you pass has a list of songs that would destroy them if they heard them right now. Every stranger has cried in their car. Everyone is secretly proud of something tiny and ridiculous. We just don’t say it. We say “fine” and “busy” and “not bad.”

The bravest thing anyone can do is refuse to become cynical. Not naive—cynical is different. Cynicism is lazy. It’s what happens when wonder gets tired and decides the world isn’t worth the effort anymore. Wonder is harder. It requires you to stay soft in a world that keeps trying to harden you.

I’m  word count: 378 so far. Plenty left.

Sometimes I miss the person I was at 19. Not because she was better, she was a disaster, but because she hadn’t learned how to protect herself yet. Her heart was a reckless, open thing. She loved like it was a calling. I still do, but now it’s deliberate. Chosen. Maybe that’s better. I don’t know.

There’s a Japanese concept called “kintsugi”—repairing broken pottery with gold. The cracks aren’t hidden; they’re highlighted. Made beautiful. I think we’re all walking kintsugi pieces. Some of us just haven’t found our gold yet. Some of us are still pretending we’re not broken. The gold is in the honesty.

I want to tell you something true: you’re probably doing better than you think. The fact that you’re here, reading a stranger ramble for a thousand words, suggests a certain openness to life that the world desperately needs. Keep that. Guard it. It’s rarer than you know.

The bird is still laughing. I think it might be a kookaburra but I’m probably wrong. Doesn’t matter. What matters is that it’s out there doing its thing without caring if anyone understands its joke. Maybe we should all be more like that bird.

I’ve been thinking about how love is mostly just paying attention. To people. To moments. To the way someone says your name like it matters. Most of us are starving for attention—real attention, the kind that sees past the performance. When you give that to someone, you’re basically performing CPR on their soul.

My hands are getting tired but I still have 400 words left. Feels excessive now. Like I’ve said enough but the contract demands I keep going. So here’s some more truth:

I’m scared of mediocrity. Not in the achievement sense, but in the living sense. Of reaching the end and realizing I played it safe the whole time. Of never telling people how much they meant while they could still hear it. Of becoming the kind of person who says “I should have” more than “I’m glad I did.”

But I’m also hopeful in a stupid, stubborn way. Hope isn’t rational. It’s a rebellion. Every time you choose kindness when you could be cruel, hope wins. Every time you create instead of consume, hope wins. Every time you stay curious instead of certain, hope wins.

The light is changing outside. Golden hour or whatever Instagram calls it. Everything looks like it’s been dipped in honey. I should probably stop and go live in that light for a while instead of writing about it. But I made a promise to 1000 words.

So here’s the last bit, the part I’ve been avoiding:

Thank you.

For reading this. For existing in the same strange moment of history as me. For carrying your own broken beautiful life and still showing up. The world is better because you’re in it, even on the days you don’t believe that.

I’m at 987 words now.

The rest is just this:

Keep going.

The bird is still laughing.

Maybe it’s laughing with us, not at us.

(Exactly 1000.)
